summary: Specifies what network devices must do to provide Controlled-Load service, which gives a flow behavior close to that of a lightly loaded network even when real traffic is heavy. It is part of the integrated services work.

eli5.summary: It is a promise that your traffic will move as if the road were nearly empty, even at rush hour.

questions: how does intserv controlled load work
how does admission control work in intserv
what does rfc 2211 require of routers
subtitle: What a router must do to give a flow the experience of a lightly loaded network, even when the network is busy.

tldr.problem: Many real-time applications work well on an unloaded network but degrade quickly when the network is overloaded, and best-effort service gives them no protection.
tldr.mechanism: A flow describes its traffic with a TSpec (a token bucket plus peak rate and packet size limits). Each network element uses admission control to accept only flows it can carry, then gives accepted flows service closely like an unloaded best-effort network.
tldr.outcome: The service is intentionally minimal, with no optional functions and no numeric delay or loss targets. Traffic that exceeds its TSpec is not dropped outright but forwarded best-effort if resources allow.

today: RFC 2211 is a Proposed Standard published in September 1997, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is meant to be used with a setup mechanism such as RSVP (see RFC 2210).

sections.title: What Controlled-Load Service Promises
sections.content:
RFC 2211 defines the requirements for network elements that support the Controlled-Load service. It is one of a series of documents that specify the network element behavior needed to support various qualities of service in IP internetworks, and it follows the service specification template given in RFC 2216.

The end-to-end promise is that a flow sees roughly what best-effort service would give it under unloaded conditions. A very high percentage of packets is delivered, with the shortfall closely approximating the basic packet error rate of the transmission medium. The transit delay for a very high percentage of delivered packets does not greatly exceed the minimum transit delay. The RFC notes that "unloaded" means not heavily loaded or congested, not that there is no other traffic at all.
sections.eli5: The network promises your messages will travel as smoothly as on a quiet day, even when everyone else is online too.

sections.title: Why a Minimal Service
sections.content:
The service is aimed at applications built for today's Internet that are highly sensitive to overload. The RFC singles out "adaptive real-time applications", which work well on unloaded networks but degrade quickly under overload. A service that mimics an unloaded network suits them.

The service is intentionally minimal. It has no optional functions or capabilities and offers a single function, so designers can assume all implementations are identical in that respect. Internally it leaves room for many scheduling and admission control techniques, from highly efficient ones to extremely simple ones.
sections.eli5: It does one job and does it the same way everywhere, like a bus that always follows the same simple rule, so everyone knows what to expect.

sections.title: What Network Elements Must Do
sections.content:
Each network element accepting a request must make sure enough bandwidth and packet processing resources exist for the requested traffic, as given by the requestor's TSpec. This must be done through active admission control, considering every important resource, such as link bandwidth, buffer space and the computational capacity of the forwarding engine.

The service takes no target values for delay or loss. Acceptance instead implies a commitment to service closely equivalent to lightly loaded best-effort. The RFC defines this by what should not happen with any frequency: little or no average queueing delay, and little or no congestion loss, over timescales significantly larger than the burst time (the time to send the flow's maximum burst at its requested rate). Any substantial sustained loss is a failure of admission control.

Elements may use statistical approaches to admission and any appropriate scheduling. There are limits, though: the implementation must have some way to "borrow" bandwidth to clear bursts, and should make extra buffering available to bursting flows because traffic is distorted as it crosses queueing points. Links must not fragment packets that receive the service; packets larger than the link MTU are treated as nonconformant. Jitter beyond the above is not required to be controlled, and losses from non-congestion causes such as link errors are not bounded.
sections.eli5: Before letting you on the fast lane, each router checks it really has room for you. If it says yes, it has to keep its word and not let the lane clog up for long.

sections.title: The TSpec and How It Is Invoked
sections.content:
The service is invoked by giving the network element the flow's traffic parameters, the TSpec. It uses the TOKEN_BUCKET_TSPEC defined in RFC 2215, which is general parameter number 127. The controlled-load service is assigned service_name 5.

  • r, the bucket rate, in bytes of IP datagrams per second, from 1 byte per second to 40 terabytes per second.
  • b, the bucket depth, in bytes, from 1 byte to 250 gigabytes.
  • p, the peak rate, with the same range as r. It exists mainly for compatibility and may always be ignored by a controlled-load element.
  • m, the minimum policed unit. Smaller datagrams are counted as size m.
  • M, the maximum packet size. A request MUST be rejected if M is larger than the link MTU. Both m and M must be positive, and m must not exceed M.

Elements MUST return an error for values outside the allowed ranges, and for in-range values they cannot support. The preferred encoding is three single-precision IEEE floating point numbers (r, b, p) followed by two 32-bit integers (m, M) in network byte order. Changing the TSpec of an existing flow is treated as a new invocation, except that a request strictly smaller than the old TSpec should never be denied.
sections.eli5: You fill in a short form about your traffic: how fast, how big the biggest burst, and how big the packets. The router checks the form and says yes or no.

sections.title: Policing and Nonconformant Traffic
sections.content:
Service is given on the basis that the flow conforms to its TSpec. Over any time period of length T, the data sent must not exceed rT+b. Packets that cause a violation of that bound, and packets bigger than the outgoing link MTU, are nonconformant.

When nonconformant packets arrive, each element must ensure locally that: (1) it MUST keep providing the contracted service to flows that are not sending excess traffic; (2) it SHOULD stop excess traffic from unfairly harming best-effort traffic; and (3) it MUST attempt to forward the excess traffic on a best-effort basis if resources are available.

Elements must not treat nonconformant traffic as unusual. Routers at the split points of a multicast tree with a shared reservation may see many packets fail the test as a matter of normal operation, and an element cannot assume upstream elements have policed the flow. The RFC permits either degrading all of a flow's packets equally, or sorting them into conformant and nonconformant sets. Putting all flows in one shared pool with no protection against nonconformant flows is insufficient.

If excess controlled-load packets are not distinguished from elastic best-effort traffic such as TCP, they can back off the elastic traffic and dominate best-effort bandwidth. The RFC says elements should have some mechanism to protect elastic traffic, but the integrated services framework does not yet address the issue.
sections.eli5: If you send more than you said you would, you are not thrown off the road. Your extra cars just have to use the slow lane, and they must not push other people aside.

sections.title: Ordering and Merging TSpecs
sections.content:
TSpec A is a substitute for TSpec B only if A's r, b, p and M are each greater than or equal to B's, and A's m is less than or equal to B's. Otherwise the two TSpecs are unordered, which can happen even when they differ.

This ordering underlies several operations used with RSVP reservations. A merged TSpec takes the largest r, b and p, the smallest m, and the smallest M. A Least Common TSpec, useful for a shared reservation made through SNMP, differs only by taking the largest M. The sum of n TSpecs, for a shared reservation of n flows, adds r, b and p, takes the minimum m and the maximum M. The minimum of two unordered TSpecs takes the smaller r, the larger b, the smaller p, the smaller m and the smaller M.
sections.eli5: When several people share one reserved lane, the router combines their forms with simple rules, such as taking the biggest speed asked for, so everyone fits.

sections.title: Guidance for Implementors
sections.content:
Admission control may oversubscribe resources: the sum of all flows' token buckets may exceed what the element can do, but only when the element is quite sure actual use is lower, for example from measurement of the aggregate flow. The most conservative approach is to reject any flow that would push the strict sum past capacity.

Section 10 suggests a two-step evaluation: compare a test flow under best-effort and under controlled-load with no load, then raise background load and watch whether loss and delay stay constant. Section 11 gives example designs: a two-level priority queue with admission control on the high-priority queue, mapping flows into an existing weighted fair queueing or class-based queueing class, or giving each flow its own weighted fair queue, which also does the policing. Excess traffic can go to a low-priority queue, a 1/N fair share of best-effort bandwidth, or be managed with RED.

Section 12 notes that the service suits applications that can characterize their traffic, such as digitized audio or video. It is not isochronous and gives no explicit delay information, so such applications still need their own timing recovery, for example with the Real-Time Transport Protocol (RFC 1889).
sections.eli5: The rules say what the router must achieve, not how. A router builder can pick a simple or a clever way, as long as the promise holds.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The service deliberately gives preferential treatment to some traffic, so whatever mechanism invokes it (RSVP, SNMP management software or proprietary control software) must be secure enough to keep unauthorized traffic from using that treatment.

A correct implementation is not open to a denial-of-service attack that requests a very small allocation for a victim's flow, because traffic above the requested level is carried best-effort rather than dropped. Giving some flows preference does mean less for others, so an attacker who reconfigures the admission control algorithm to overallocate could starve other flows. The RFC argues this adds little risk, since many other router reconfigurations can cause denial of service, and the protection against those should cover this too.
sections.eli5: Only people allowed to use the fast lane should get in. And because extra traffic is slowed rather than banned, a trickster cannot easily cut you off.
